Specifically: WUE = Annual water usage (L) / Server equipment energy (kWh) [16] 11 According to a 2016 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) report, it takes about 7.6 liters of water on average to generate 1kWh of energy in the US, while an average data center has a WUE of 1.8 L/kWh (7.9 gpm/MW). The result is US data centers consume billions of liters of water each year and the amount of water usage is growing [10]. For example, it was reported2 that Google data centers in The Dalles, Oregon consumed more than 355 million gallons of water in 2021 — an amount that had tripled since 2016 — representing more than one-quarter of the town’s annual water consumption. Two more data centers are slated to come online in the future, adding to the regional water demand [14]. Another study in 2016 by the Uptime Institute [22] put data center water usage at 12.8 gpm/MW for a standard water chiller system and cooling tower, which translates to a WUE of 2.9 L/kWh. Cooling towers require makeup water because of evaporation, blow down, and drift. The report noted that there are techniques, technologies, and temperature tolerances that can reduce the cooling water requirement per MW of data center load. Since 2016, data centers have committed to better tracking of water usage and improvements in efficiency. In addition, more water-neutral renewable energy sources have come online. An updated 2024 LBNL report indicates that data centers in the US have a WUE of 0.36 L/kWh (1.6 gpm/MW) through 2023. After 2023, the average data center WUE is projected to rise to a value of 0.45 to 0.48 L/kWh (2.1 gpm/MW), reflecting increasing construction of hyperscale and Collocation data centers [17]. The 2024 LBNL report notes that US data centers consumed approximately 176 TWh in 2023 using nearly 800 billion liters of water for electricity generation based on the regional electricity grid mix for data center locations. This translates to a national average of 4.52 L/kWh (20 gpm/MW) of indirect water consumption for data centers [17]. This indicates as much as 5.0 L/kWh (22 gpm/MW) total direct and indirect water consumption for new data centers. A collocated small, advanced NPP to directly power the data center can project the cooling water requirements of the NPP and the projected needs of a hyperscale or collection of data centers. Direct data center water consumption occurs close to the data center site while the associated indirect water consumption is distributed more broadly geographically. Therefore, data center site selection should consider the potential stress on the local water basin associated with the potential site [11]. Data center cooling sources could be freshwater lakes and streams, freshwater aquafers, local water distribution systems, or reprocessed water (municipal gray water). Onsite purification will likely be required because of the ultrapure need for data center cooling. 3.3 Access to Fiber or Connectivity Fiber infrastructure is becoming widespread in developed areas such as urban and suburban locations.
